hypotheticals.question: Whether BNS s. 35 (Right of private defence of body and of property) applies, and how structured written arguments should be framed.
hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 35 (Right of private defence of body and of property), Chapter III — General Exceptions.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) Every person has a right, subject to the restrictions contained in section 37, to defend—
   (2) (a) his own body, and the body of any other person, against any offence affecting the human body;
   (3) (b) the property, whether movable or immovable, of himself or of any other person, against any act which is an offence falling under the definition of theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass, or which is an attempt to commit theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 35 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 35 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

learningObjectives: Analyze the twin domains of private defence under BNS s. 35: body and property.
Understand that the right protects not only one's own body/property but also that of any other person.
Identify the specific property offences that trigger the right of private defence.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 35 provides that every person has a right, subject to the restrictions contained in section 37, to defend: (First) — His own body, and the body of any other person, against any offence affecting the human body; (Secondly) — The property, whether movable or immovable, of himself or of any other person, against any act which is an offence falling under the definition of theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass, or which is an attempt to commit theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The right of private defence in Indian criminal law embodies broad civic solidarity. It is not selfish: a citizen is entitled by law to defend not only himself, but any fellow human being from bodily offences, and to defend anyone's property from theft, robbery, mischief, or criminal trespass.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 35 (corresponding to IPC s. 97).
Overriding caveat: 'subject to the restrictions contained in section 37'.
Limb 1 (Body): Defend own body + body of ANY OTHER person against ANY offence affecting the human body.
Limb 2 (Property): Defend property (movable/immovable) of oneself + of ANY OTHER person against theft, robbery, mischief, or criminal trespass (or attempts).
essentialIngredients: There is an act or attempt which constitutes an offence affecting the human body, OR an offence of theft, robbery, mischief, or criminal trespass.
The defence is exercised to protect oneself or any other person.
The exercise is strictly subject to the restrictions in s. 37 (recourse to authorities, proportionality, public servant exception).
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 35 marks a glorious expansion of the right of self-defence into an affirmative civic duty. A bystander who witnesses a woman being assaulted on the street is equally entitled to use force in her defence as the victim herself. Similarly, a person who sees a burglar breaking into a neighbor's house has a full legal right to intervene and defend the neighbor's property. The property defended may be movable (money, cattle, cars) or immovable (houses, land). The offences against property giving rise to this right are strictly four: theft, robbery, mischief, and criminal trespass, along with their attempts.
examples: Teaching example (Defending a stranger): A passerby sees an armed assailant attempting to stab an unknown pedestrian. The passerby strikes the assailant with a heavy staff, fracturing his arm. Section 35 protects the passerby because the right extends to defending 'the body of any other person'.

Teaching example (Defending neighbor's farm): A farmer sees trespassers cutting down a neighbor's standing timber at night (theft/mischief). The farmer intervenes with necessary force to drive them away. Section 35 protects the farmer.
distinctions: Defence of own person vs Defence of others: Both are placed on exactly equal legal footing under s. 35.
Bodily offences vs Property offences: Bodily defence arises against 'any offence affecting the human body'; property defence is restricted strictly to theft, robbery, mischief, and criminal trespass.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a passerby who injured an assailant while rescuing a stranger from an ongoing robbery can claim private defence under BNS s. 35.
Rule: Section 35 allows any person to defend the body and property of any other person against robbery and bodily offences, subject to s. 37.
Application: Check whether the attack on the stranger was unlawful, whether the rescuer had time to call police, and whether force used was proportionate.
Conclusion: If within s. 37 limits, s. 35 completely shields the rescuer.
